newsitem.title: EGYPT: Privatisation talk puts Egypt state banks on alert.
newsitem.headline: Privatisation talk puts Egypt state banks on alert.

text.p: Egypt's public-sector banks are under unprecedented scrutiny this year as the government weighs the advantages of breaking the cosy links of the past 30 years.

Privatising one of the four big retail banks is on the agenda at last -- tentatively at this stage because of political sensitivities about the state giving up control of the financial sector, especially to foreigners.
A central bank official has said the state will sell off one of the banks in full by the end of the year but others say they doubt bank privatisation at that rate is feasible.
"When it comes to the banks, you're talking about selling the family silver. It won't be easy," one economist said.
"They are floating a balloon and encouraging people to discuss it. They are preparing the ground so people will accept it," added Mohamed Abdullah of brokerage Intercapital.
The government has not said which bank it is targeting, creating unease among bank workers who fear mass redundancies and want to know where their bank stands in the timetable.
But a bigger obstacle, bankers say, is the secrecy surrounding the true state of the banks' balance sheets, which carry a long legacy of state interference in their operations.

Economists estimate that "non-performing" loans -- the euphemism for bad debts -- may account for more than 30 percent of the banks' total loan portfolios, reducing their appeal to potential investors.

The central bank says the banks have made adequate provision for these loans but the banks' own figures show that the provisions, some of them for possible tax liabilities, are equivalent to only 17 percent of total loans.

After bank nationalisation in the 1960s, the four retail banks -- National Bank of Egypt, Banque Misr, Banque du Caire and Bank of Alexandria -- became mere instruments of state policy, obeying government diktats on interest rates, foreign exchange dealings and investment priorities.
In return the state sheltered them from competition by requiring that public sector companies use their services and restricting licences for new private-sector banks.
The picture has changed with gradual liberalisation in the 1990s but the state banks continue to dominate, especially outside the cities, where few other banks have branches.
The concept of state banks as charities rather than independent businesses persists in government circles.

"The Egyptian banking system has responsibilities and a role in development," said Banque Misr chairman Essam el-Ahmadi. "We (Egypt) are about to embark on giant projects. Who is going to finance them?" he said in a newspaper interview.
"Can we leave the national economy to its fate?" added Mohamed el-Asfar, former chairman of Alexandria Kuwait International Bank, a joint-venture bank.
"The private sector aims for quick profit and has no interest in the national economy... The public-sector banks answer the needs of society," he added.
Judging by the previous phases of the privatisation programme, in which performance fell far behind forecasts, it might be premature to expect action by the end of year.
There is also no consensus yet on the method the government would adopt in privatising one of the banks.

Central Bank sub-governor Faika el-Rifaie told Reuters the plan was to sell 40 to 60 percent of the equity to an anchor investor and to invite foreign banks to take a stake. But state-bank executives are sceptical about that method.
Mahmoud Abdel-Aziz, chairman of National Bank of Egypt, the biggest of the state banks, said on Monday that an outright sale would not be the right way.
"We need to increase capital, which can be done by the private sector. We can invite the private sector to join or go into a merger but not a total sale," he told reporters.
